{"id": "38:6/q01", "question": "What does انطلق mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the departure is physical or figurative speech.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q01/p1", "position": "It means to depart or go away.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares ذهب and انطلق. {"id": "38:6/q03", "question": "Who are the الملأ?", "turns_on": "The reported count and roster vary.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q03/p1", "position": "They are Quraysh's notables and leaders.", "reasons": "Muqātil counts twenty-seven and names al-Walīd, Abū Jahl, Umayya and Ubayy. Itqān and Ālūsī give differing rosters. {"id": "38:6/q04", "question": "Who voiced the command?", "turns_on": "Whether the counsel was collective or traced to an individual.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q04/p1", "position": "The chiefs spoke among themselves or to their followers.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda expands compressed speech as mutual counsel, call or urging. {"id": "38:6/q05", "question": "What does منهم identify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q05/p1", "position": "The chiefs belong to Quraysh, distinguished from lesser followers.", "reasons": "Rāzī explicitly says Quraysh; Biqāʿī distinguishes their elite from followers and outsiders."}]}
{"id": "38:6/q06", "question": "How is أن امشوا constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether أن explains implied speech or is governed as a source expression.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q06/p1", "position": "أن is explanatory, like أي, introducing implied speech without case.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl via Sībawayh says they went out saying Go, comparing 5:117. Abū ʿUbayda, Zajjāj, Wāḥidī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī supply a saying verb. Ibn ʿAṭiyya denies case position. Zamakhsharī via Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn, with Bayḍāwī and Nasafī, reasons that departure from debate implies speech. Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn also supply a circumstantial conversation; others make departure itself speech. Ibn ʿĀshūr supports both with 38:4–5. Al-Ṣaffār in Burhān prefers explanation because a bare noun cannot be a speech complement unless the utterance itself."}, {"id": "38:6/q06/p2", "position": "أن is source-forming or accusative, with an implied bi.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī attaches accusative أن to انطلقوا. Samīn also permits a verbal noun governed by an omitted circumstantial clause."}, {"id": "38:6/q06/p3", "position": "An omitted verb of saying precedes the command.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda expands it as mutual advice or call; Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Abū Isḥāq supply 'saying'."}]}
{"id": "38:6/q07", "question": "What variant wording or pronunciation is reported?", "turns_on": "The transmitted wording and pause pronunciation.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q07/p1", "position": "The common reading has أن امشوا; restart امشوا with kasra after a pause.", "reasons": "Samīn and Biqāʿī derive the kasra from the original third-letter vowel; Biqāʿī contrasts the feminine ḍamma."}, {"id": "38:6/q07/p2", "position": "Ibn Abī ʿAbla omits أن.", "reasons": "Rāzī names him; Bayḍāwī reports the form."}, {"id": "38:6/q07/p3", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd reads that the chiefs left walking, then said to persevere.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives وانطلق الملأ منهم يمشون أن اصبروا. {"id": "38:6/q08", "question": "What does امشوا command?", "turns_on": "Whether it signals literal movement, a continuing way, multiplication, or a prayer; Khaṭṭābī disputes its stylistic force.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q08/p1", "position": "Walk away from the gathering or leave the Prophet's presence.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as go. Abū Isḥāq has them disperse from Abū Ṭālib's meeting. Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī take literal steps out; Samīn calls ordinary walking primary. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn ʿĀshūr allow a literal order."}, {"id": "38:6/q08/p2", "position": "Continue in inherited religion and opposition to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Māwardī cites the idiom 'walk on a matter' for adherence. Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers 'continue on your path'; Rāzī says they saw no way to stop Muhammad. Khaṭṭābī says calm 'walk on' suits familiar steady practice, while 'go forth' would imply agitation. Zamakhsharī, followed by others, compares a prolific woman and the auspicious livestock word."}, {"id": "38:6/q08/p5", "position": "It is a prayer for abundant cattle.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it grammatically weak and contextually unsuitable. Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn and Ālūsī say livestock أمشى requires hamzat al-qaṭʿ; Ālūsī calls the sense remote."}, {"id": "38:6/q08/p6", "position": "The word is weaker than 'proceed' or 'go forth'.", "reasons": "Khaṭṭābī reports this objection to its expressive force."}]}
{"id": "38:6/q09", "question": "What does 'be patient over your gods' mean?", "turns_on": "How ṣabr and ʿalā express persistence.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q09/p1", "position": "Persist in worship and loyalty to their gods despite criticism.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Damghānī and Ibn ʿĀshūr compare 25:42. Ibn ʿĀshūr traces ṣabr to tying an animal, then composure in hardship; ʿalā figuratively marks established adherence with worship implied, contrasting 73:10 and 68:48 and comparing 2:5. Bursawī and Ālūsī specify enduring disparagement; Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses not abandoning worship. Iṣlāḥī describes fidelity to ancestral religion until death."}]}
{"id": "38:6/q10", "question": "What lesson is drawn from the chiefs' patience?", "turns_on": "Whether the example is used to condemn idolatry or exhort believers.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q10/p1", "position": "Their persistence in idolatry is censured.", "reasons": "Sahl distinguishes patience in obedience, pain and suffering from persistence in disobedience. Burhān says continued idolatry ends in the Fire, citing 25:75."}, {"id": "38:6/q10/p2", "position": "Believers have greater reason to persevere in worship.", "reasons": "ʿUmar reproaches believers who abandon patience. Al-Qushayrī and Taʾwīlāt Najmiyya compare believers' resolve with idolaters'; the latter extends it to lovers seeking the Beloved."}]}

{"id": "38:6/q13", "question": "What episode prompted the chiefs' words?", "turns_on": "The notes give a council occasion, a chronology after ʿUmar's conversion, a later application at Badr, and a sequel.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q13/p1", "position": "Quraysh's delegation sought Abū Ṭālib's intervention, rejected the one-word confession, and left.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Wāḥidī and Durr makes the visit the occasion. Muqātil gives their arbitration request, Abū Ṭālib's summons, proposed mutual noninterference, Muhammad's single word promising Arab obedience and non-Arab submission, Abū Jahl's offer of ten, and their recoil from one God. Al-Suddī says they feared Arab reproach if they attacked after Abū Ṭālib died. Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes versions differ: one adds an offer of earth's gold, another the sun and moon. Kuran Yolu says prior ridicule failed; Durr includes a threat to Muhammad and his Lord and mentions 38:7."}, {"id": "38:6/q13/p2", "position": "The affair followed ʿUmar's conversion and growth of the Muslims.", "reasons": "Muqātil via Māwardī and Qurṭubī links the remark to ʿUmar. Wāḥidī's commentators say Quraysh then asked Muhammad to abandon his God and their idols; Baghawī stresses Muslim growth."}, {"id": "38:6/q13/p3", "position": "At Badr the Prophet applied the verse to enemy chiefs.", "reasons": "Abū Mijlaz reports that a man called them women; the Prophet corrected him, called them chiefs and recited the verse."}, {"id": "38:6/q13/p4", "position": "Afterward Muhammad urged Abū Ṭālib to confess God's oneness, but he refused.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says Abū Ṭālib feared Arabs would attribute conversion to fear of death. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he feared descendants' blame and died on ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib's religion."}]}
{"id": "38:6/q14", "question": "How does the verse connect to the sūra and other passages?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q14/p1", "position": "The chiefs' rejection continues the sūra's account of arrogant resistance to monotheism.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says Ṣād shares its group's foundation in divine oneness: 1–11 presents the reminder rejected from arrogance like earlier nations, with a messenger from among Quraysh called sorcerer and liar. Kuran Yolu says monotheism threatened their traditions, status and interests. Study Quran points to 34:34 for notables' rejection."}, {"id": "38:6/q14/p2", "position": "The Abū Ṭālib episode also relates to 28:56.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn Kathīr tie Abū Ṭālib's refusal to profess faith to 28:56."}]}
{"id": "38:6/q15", "question": "What ancillary linguistic observations accompany citations of this verse?", "turns_on": "These are grammatical and linguistic comparisons preserved in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "38:6/q15/p1", "position": "Arabic has distinct forms with distinct meanings, synonyms, and polysemous forms.", "reasons": "Sībawayh contrasts جلس and ذهب; ذهب and انطلق share a sense; وجد عليه means resentment whereas وجد can mean finding a lost thing."}, {"id": "38:6/q15/p2", "position": "Derived انطلق illustrates initial kasra in related imperfect patterns.", "reasons": "Sībawayh traces prefix kasra by analogy with forms beginning in hamzat al-waṣl, whose alif was omitted for ease."}, {"id": "38:6/q15/p3", "position": "A definite and indefinite noun, or nouns under incompatible governors, cannot share one adjective; a new clause or accusative praise resolves it.", "reasons": "Sībawayh permits قائمين for a man and the pronoun in معه, implicit with مع امرأة; he bars shared adjectives for mismatched case, definiteness, nested annexations such as أخوى ابنين and أخوى ابنيك, or a known and unknown referent, while matching subject relations allow one. الرجلان الصالحان can start a sentence or be accusative praise, like al-Kharnāq's النازلين and الطيبون; the accusative is not ḥāl because an article-bearing adjective cannot be ḥāl. It can mark insult. Al-Khalīl rejects ناقة وفصيلها الراتعان and mismatched governors, and reads أنفسهما as fresh nominative identification or accusative 'I mean them,' not praise."}, {"id": "38:6/q15/p4", "position": "Independent إن after حتى differs from subordinate أن, and lightened or heavy أن may retain an implied pronoun.", "reasons": "Sībawayh makes إن after حتى an independent clause, not a subordinate noun; he compares فإذا إنه and an alternative فإذا أنه for a state of servitude. Al-Khalīl permits حتى أنك أحمق as حتى حمقك but rejects كما أنك on the pattern كما أنت. At 10:10 and 24:9 Sībawayh makes heavy أن with an omitted pronoun; at 37:104–105 he allows أنك قد صدقت while al-Khalīl also permits explanatory أي. Poetic lightened كأن وريديه and أن هالك retain governing force; nominative كأن وريداه or an إنما/لكن analysis is also possible. He supplies a pronoun in أن بسم الله and argues from the awkwardness of أن يقول ذاك without a negative or future marker."}, {"id": "38:6/q15/p5", "position": "Elsewhere أن with an imperative can be subjunctive, while explanatory أن resembles this verse.", "reasons": "Sībawayh analyzes كتبت إليه أن افعل and أمرته أن قم with subjunctive أن linked to an imperative, supported by أوعزت إليه بأن افعل where a preposition attaches as to a noun; he also offers explanatory أي in the comparison."}, {"id": "38:6/q15/p6", "position": "The Qurʾān's clear Arabic permits plain eloquence, and a cited discussion proposes several ellipses.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda cites 14:4 for revelation in the audience's language and says early Arabs needed no explanation. Khaṭṭābī values grandeur, sweetness and ease over harsh obscurity. Nashr gives omitted replies such as 'you have surely been brought' or 'it is surely a miracle.' Itqān says its cited work details unnamed peoples, animals, places and times."}]}

Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes everything he reports from God, and al-Samin specifies the teaching of divine oneness in the proposed end-time faith."}, {"id": "38:7/q01/p3", "position": "The account of the Arabs' earlier monotheist history and origins.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says prophetic history from Noah to Abraham, Abraham and Ishmael's settlement in Arabia, and the Kaaba's original purpose challenged Quraysh's account of its ancestry; Quraysh called that account fabricated because their later history and inherited reports lacked it."}]}
{"id": "38:7/q02", "question": "How does their claim of never hearing this express their objection?", "turns_on": "Whether inherited silence is taken as evidence against the claim or the word 'later' itself concedes an earlier tradition.", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q02/p1", "position": "They infer that an unheard doctrine is invented, appealing to inherited custom; the inference is unsound.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the denial of hearing signals rejection and accusation, and can explain their previous assertion that the matter is contrived; bi-hādhā implies 'anything like this,' while repeating the demonstrative marks the claim distinctly. Al-Rāzī says treating ancestral silence as proof exposes invalid taqlīd. Bursevī calls following ancestral error ignorant and quotes a Persian warning that an apparent route to the Kaaba may lead to Turkistan. Al-Biqāʿī says reflection can disclose monotheism even without inherited testimony. Study Quran's R says their premise was that a message unheard among predecessors must be false; Iṣlāḥī says they demanded ancestral transmission of the earlier history."}, {"id": "38:7/q02/p2", "position": "Their restriction to the later religion implies awareness of monotheism in the earlier Abrahamic tradition.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says Abraham and his descendants knew oneness before ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy; they also knew resurrection. He cites ʿUbayd ibn al-Abraṣ's line about the displaced Banū Asad serving until resurrection, with Ibn al-Furāt's account of Ḥujr ibn ʿAmr's campaign as its background. Reports from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās identify ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir or ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy as the first idolater or changer of Abraham's religion; at Mecca the Prophet rejected images of Abraham and Ishmael holding divining arrows."}]}
{"id": "38:7/q03", "question": "What does milla mean here, and how is it used of pagan custom?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q03/p1", "position": "It means religion; applying it to inherited polytheist custom is figurative usage.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd glosses milla as religion. Bursevī says its proper use, like dīn, is the divine law prescribed through prophets for reward and nearness; the pagan application is analogical."}]}
{"id": "38:7/q04", "question": "What can ākhira mean in this phrase and elsewhere?", "turns_on": "The contextual referent of a relative word meaning what comes after; the other senses are illustrated by other Qur'anic contexts.", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q04/p1", "position": "Later or last: a thing following another of its kind.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd calls it the other or later religion; al-Dāmghānī says latest prior community or the later of two punishments. Ibn al-Jawzī explains that al-ākhir has something before it, and notes uses for 'finally,' a group's rear, and a saddle's back. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls ākhira the feminine of ākhir and cites the later creation in 29:20."}, {"id": "38:7/q04/p2", "position": "The Resurrection or Last Day.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites 2:4 and 27:3."}, {"id": "38:7/q04/p3", "position": "Paradise or the lasting reward of the God-conscious.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites 2:102, 28:83, 43:35 and 42:20."}, {"id": "38:7/q04/p4", "position": "Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites the worshipper fearing the Hereafter while hoping for mercy in 39:9."}, {"id": "38:7/q04/p5", "position": "The grave or life after death.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites God's making believers firm in this life and the next, 14:27."}, {"id": "38:7/q04/p6", "position": "The final punishment or destruction of the Israelites.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites 17:7."}]}
{"id": "38:7/q05", "question": "Which religion or period is 'the later religion'?", "turns_on": "Whether 'later' points to the last scriptural community, the speakers' own or contemporary tradition, a future community, or a different historical period; the notes test these against context, ancestral practice and the opponents' knowledge of Christianity.", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q05/p1", "position": "Christianity, the last prior religious community or religion of Jesus.", "reasons": "Mujāhid is transmitted both for and against this identification. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Quraẓī/Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Kalbī, Muqātil, al-Suddī and others are also named. Muqātil, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı and Ibn ʿĀshūr say Christians' Trinity or association of another god made the opponents claim not to have heard monotheism there; al-Ālūsī rejects attributing this belief to Jesus himself. Al-Ṭabarī's Ibn ʿAbbās report and al-Durr's Mujāhid report say Quraysh argued Christians would have told them if the Qur'an were true. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that Christianity had little standing among Quraysh; Iṣlāḥī says the context would support it only if they believed in Christianity or Muhammad based his call on it."}, {"id": "38:7/q05/p2", "position": "Quraysh's own inherited religion or Arab custom in their time.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Qatāda are commonly cited; Qatāda adds their own era, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes Arab tradition. Al-Wāḥidī calls it their forefathers' religion. Bursevī says their tradition followed earlier religions. Ibn ʿĀshūr adduces the Abū Ṭālib deathbed question about ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib's religion. Iṣlāḥī connects it to the absence of monotheism from later Arab history. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī extends it to accepted later or near-contemporary peoples' religions, contrasted with ancient tales."}, {"id": "38:7/q05/p3", "position": "Judaism and Christianity, and possibly the inherited ancestral tradition, taken together.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says leaders found no such teaching in Christianity, Judaism or their fathers' tradition. Ibn al-Jawzī transmits al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj: Jews associated ʿUzayr with God and Christians professed three in one."}, {"id": "38:7/q05/p4", "position": "The interval between Jesus and Muhammad, or their own historical time.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥakam identifies the period between Jesus and Muhammad; al-Ḥasan and Qatāda instead phrase the objection as not having heard this arise in their time. These reports vary on the period's limits."}, {"id": "38:7/q05/p5", "position": "A coming end-time religion or prophet whose monotheism they claim no one foretold.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites anticipations by monks, Shīq, Saṭīḥ and Israelites. Al-Ḥasan says they claimed not to have heard such an end-time event would occur. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Samin name scriptural scholars and soothsayers as alleged silent witnesses; al-Samin calls the assertion an extreme lie. Al-Ālūsī reads the phrase circumstantially and says the monotheist, idol-breaking prophet was in fact widely expected."}, {"id": "38:7/q05/p6", "position": "The People of the Book's testimony to Muhammad's prophethood, allegedly absent.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and Kur'an Yolu give this as an alternative paraphrase: Quraysh had heard nothing from Jews and Christians affirming Muhammad as a true messenger."}, {"id": "38:7/q05/p7", "position": "The first pre-Islamic religion, through a claimed Coptic reversal of first and last.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī reports the claim that Copts call the first 'last' and the last 'first'; al-Suyūṭī transmits Shīdhala's identification of the first pre-Islamic religion by the same explanation."}, {"id": "38:7/q05/p8", "position": "Religions current in the speakers' later age, including Christianity and other plural or incarnate divinities.", "reasons": "Asad's 'faiths of latter days' includes Christianity's Trinity and Hinduism's triad. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī similarly contrasts contemporary or near-contemporary accepted religion with ancient peoples' tales, though he rejects singling out Christianity."}]}

{"id": "38:7/q08", "question": "What force does in have in 'in hādhā illā ikhtilāq'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q08/p1", "position": "It is negative, equivalent to mā: 'this is only fabrication.'", "reasons": "Bursevī explicitly identifies in as a negator; the following illā restricts the predicate to fabrication."}]}
{"id": "38:7/q09", "question": "What does ikhtilāq mean in their accusation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q09/p1", "position": "A lie or invented falsehood, alleged to have been made up by Muhammad himself.", "reasons": "Al-Walīd makes the personal accusation; al-Ṭabarī's Ibn ʿAbbās says false conjecture, while Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd give lie or something made up. {"id": "38:7/q10", "question": "What occasion is reported for these verses?", "turns_on": "The reports give different triggers: Abū Ṭālib's illness and the leaders' appeal, or their agitation after ʿUmar's conversion.", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q10/p1", "position": "During Abū Ṭālib's illness, Quraysh leaders sought to stop Muhammad's criticism of their gods, and rejected his request for the declaration of God's oneness.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī names Abū Jahl, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth, and says the elders feared Arab reproach if they attacked after Abū Ṭālib's death. Muhammad promised a word yielding Arab allegiance and rule over non-Arabs; the leaders rejected 'There is no god but God' and left angry. Ibn ʿAbbās's report in al-Wāḥidī and al-Biqāʿī gives the illness and the one word; al-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Study Quran's IK/Q/R/Ṭ report says Arab allegiance and non-Arab tribute and that the chiefs scoffed they would say ten declarations; its IJ report connects the event to 38:1–7. Ibn al-Jawzī also identifies the opening through 38:7 with this episode."}, {"id": "38:7/q10/p2", "position": "After ʿUmar's conversion, Quraysh sought a compromise over gods and idols; the Prophet called them to one God and they refused.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī transmits this account from the commentators as another setting in which the verses followed."}]}
{"id": "38:7/q11", "question": "What happened when Muhammad urged Abū Ṭālib himself to profess God's oneness?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q11/p1", "position": "Abū Ṭālib refused from fear that Arabs would say he yielded at death and remained with his forefathers' religion; 28:56 followed.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī reports the deathbed appeal and refusal, then the revelation 'You do not guide whom you love' (28:56). {"id": "38:7/q12", "question": "Were people between prophets excused for lacking knowledge of monotheism?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q12/p1", "position": "No; the earlier divine message was available and people could be held responsible.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says reports about the introduction of idols and Abraham's actual practice refute blanket ignorance in the interval, while 17:15 bears on the issue. {"id": "38:7/q13", "question": "What does their statement reveal about their motive?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q13/p1", "position": "It reveals envy and resistance to Muhammad's revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās calls the speakers envious. {"id": "38:7/q14", "question": "How does this rejection fit the opening of Sūrat Ṣād?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q14/p1", "position": "The opening presents proud Quraysh rejecting the reminder of tawḥīd as earlier nations did, until belief comes too late.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says Ṣād, like preceding sūrahs in its group, is founded on tawḥīd; 38:1–11 show a reminder opposed through arrogance and polytheism and parallel prior nations. {"id": "38:7/q15", "question": "Can the Qur'an have been fabricated by alteration or loss?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q15/p1", "position": "No; divine preservation and public transmission make alteration or concealment untenable.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī cites God's guarantee, including 41:42, and multitudes across places and circumstances who memorized the Qur'an for recitation, law, exegesis, eloquence and scrutiny. {"id": "38:7/q16", "question": "What in the Qur'an supports its divine source against the charge of invention?", "turns_on": "Whether Qur'anic form belongs to a known speech form, and whether its reports could have come from ordinary learning.", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q16/p1", "position": "Its distinctive order and reports of unseen earlier events support Muhammad's prophethood.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī says reports of unseen earlier events are evidence because Muhammad neither learned them from scripture nor witnessed them; he cites 29:48, 28:44, 28:46 and 11:49. Its style differs from ordinary prophetic speech, as two men's sermons differ, and falls outside familiar patterns. He says one must rule out poetry, sajʿ and metrical speech, which takes reflective, acquired discernment. Disagreement among believers about the route of proof does not nullify proof, just as arguments for the world's origination differ."}, {"id": "38:7/q16/p2", "position": "It is poetry, according to some Quraysh opponents, or contains poetry, according to some heretics.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports both claims as forms he argues must be excluded to establish the Qur'an's exceptional order."}, {"id": "38:7/q16/p3", "position": "It is rhymed prose, albeit more eloquent than ordinary sajʿ.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports this description from some Muslims while arguing that its order lies outside familiar speech forms."}, {"id": "38:7/q16/p4", "position": "It is metrical speech, hence within familiar discourse.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports the claim as another form to be excluded in his proof."}]}
{"id": "38:7/q17", "question": "Which passage was the last revelation?", "turns_on": "Whether 'last' means the final revelation absolutely or the latest each authority personally heard.", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q17/p1", "position": "Sūrat al-Naṣr.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports Ibn ʿAbbās's identification, 110:1."}, {"id": "38:7/q17/p2", "position": "Sūrat al-Māʾida.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports ʿĀʾisha's identification, 5:1."}, {"id": "38:7/q17/p3", "position": "Sūrat Barāʾa.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib's identification, 9:1."}, {"id": "38:7/q17/p4", "position": "The verse of return to God, 2:281.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's identification."}, {"id": "38:7/q17/p5", "position": "The instruction to say 'God is sufficient for me,' 9:129.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports al-Suddī's identification."}, {"id": "38:7/q17/p6", "position": "The reports can differ because each reporter identified the last passage he heard personally.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī says disagreement over placement or last hearing does not entail disagreement about the Qur'an's divine source; he compares the reports for 110:1, 5:1, 9:1, 2:281 and 9:129."}]}

{"id": "38:7/q19", "question": "What function are the disconnected letters said to serve?", "turns_on": "Whether the letters work as attention signals or numerical signs; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ traces the latter reports to a disputed narrative setting.", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q19/p1", "position": "They catch listeners' attention and prompt them to listen to the revelation that follows.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports that unfamiliar letters are not mistaken for a complete statement. {"id": "38:7/q20", "question": "What broader knowledge is said to have been derived from the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "38:7/q20/p1", "position": "People derived timekeeping, literary sciences and inward terminology from its language and verses.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī reports timekeeping from day, night, sun, moon, phases, stars and constellations; writers and poets derived semantics and rhetorical sciences from eloquence, arrangement, openings, endings and shifts of address; people of spiritual allusion derived terms including annihilation, abiding, presence, fear, awe, intimacy, estrangement, contraction and expansion."}]}

{"id": "39:6/q01", "question": "Who is the single soul from which humanity was created?", "turns_on": "Whether 'one soul' identifies the first person, the human kind, or an inward principle.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q01/p1", "position": "Adam, the common origin of humankind.", "reasons": "Muqatil and many others name Adam; al-Tabari cites 2:21 and 4:1, Ibn Kathir notes diverse languages and colors from one origin, and Study Quran cites 4:1, 6:98, 7:189, and 31:28. {"id": "39:6/q03", "question": "What sequence does 'then He made from it its mate' express?", "turns_on": "Whether the sequence is chronological, orders narration or foreknowledge, or ranks two signs.", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q03/p1", "position": "It orders the report or discourse, though Eve was created before Adam's descendants.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Farra via Ibn al-Jawzi, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, and Suyuti cite normal Arabic reporting later-mentioned earlier events; Ibn Atiyya adduces Abu Nuwas's father and grandfather verse, while Tabrisi cites poetry. Suyuti rejects redundant thumma and says an omitted clause explains 9:118; Ibn Hisham says discourse order does not explain delay. Tabataba'i calls the sequence rhetorical."}, {"id": "39:6/q03/p2", "position": "It is temporal: Adam's descendants were extracted as particles before Eve was created.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari cites a Prophetic report of all future souls from Adam's back and Companion reports, preferring this account; others report it. Zajjaj says Eve was made before the rest of humanity."}, {"id": "39:6/q03/p4", "position": "It marks the higher rank of Eve's exceptional creation as a sign, rather than elapsed time.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari via Abu Hayyan and Samin treats Eve's creation from Adam's body as more striking. {"id": "39:6/q04", "question": "Why does this verse say 'created you' rather than another creation verb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:6/q04/p1", "position": "The verb suits this surah's context and repeated vocabulary.", "reasons": "Samarrai compares al-Anam's أنشأكم with خلقكم in al-Nisa, al-Araf, and al-Zumar; each choice fits its setting."}]}
